At the same time it must be noted that, had the Lord not begun to fast, the devil would have had no occasion to tempt, according to that saying: Son, as you come to the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation. …
4:40: When evening had come, they brought to him many who had demons, and he cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were ill. All are healed not in the morning, not at midday, but towards evening, when the sun is about to set, when the grain of wheat dies in the earth that it may bear much fruit.
4:5: Again the devil takes him up onto a very high mountain and shows him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. The glory of the world, which is to pass away with the world, is displayed on a mountain and on a height. But the Lord comes down to low places and plains, so as to overcome the devil by humility. …
4:6: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER FOUR

[Daniel 4:4] "I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at ease in my house and prospering in my palace." The narrative is clear indeed and requires but little interpretation. Because he displeased God, Nebuchadnezzar was turned into a madman and dwelt for seven years amongst the brute beasts and was fed upon the roots of herbs, Afterwards by the mercy of God he was restored to his throne, and praised and glorified the King of heaven, on the ground that all His works are truth and His ways are justice and He is able to abase those …
4:8: Then Jesus said to him: Go, Satan; it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God and him alone shall you serve. Satan and the apostle Peter are not, as most think, condemned by the same sentence. For to Peter it is said: Go behind me, Satan, that is, follow me, you who are contrary to my will; but here he hears: go, Satan, and behind is not said to him, so that it is understood: go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for you and your angels.
5:12: And when he had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. And behold, a leper came and worshiped him. As the Lord comes down from the mountain the crowds meet him, because they had not been able to ascend to the higher places. And the first to meet him is the leper. For with his leprosy he could not yet hear the Savior's so manifold discourse on the mountain. …
5:13: And Jesus, stretching out his hand, touched him, saying: I will, be cleansed. As the Lord stretches out his hand, at once the leprosy flees. At the same time consider how humble and free of boasting the answer is. The one had said: If you will; the Lord answered: I will; the one had put first: you can cleanse me; the Lord joins it and says: be cleansed. So it is not to be joined and read, as most of the Latins think: I will to cleanse, but separately, so that first he says: I will, and then commands: be cleansed.
6:10: Then he said to the man: Stretch out your hand. And he stretched it out, and it was restored to health like the other. In the Gospel which the Nazarenes and the Ebionites use, which we recently translated from the Hebrew language into Greek, and which is called by most the authentic Matthew, this man who has the withered hand is described as a mason, begging for help in words of this kind: I was a mason, seeking my living with my hands; I beg you, Jesus, to restore my health to me, so that I may not shamefully beg …
6:14: First, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother. To set out the order of the apostles and the merit of each belonged to him who searches the secrets of the heart. Simon, surnamed Peter, is written first, to distinguish him from the other Simon, who is called the Cananaean, from Cana, the village of Galilee where the Lord turned water into wine. He also calls James the son of Zebedee, because another James follows as well, the son of Alphaeus. And he joins the apostles together in pairs and yokes. …
6:15: Simon the Cananaean. He is the one who in another evangelist is written as zelotes; for Cana is interpreted 'zeal'. The history of the Church relates that the apostle Thaddaeus was sent to Edessa, to Abgar king of Osrhoene; he is called Judas of James by the evangelist Luke, and elsewhere he is named Lebbaeus, which is interpreted 'little heart'; and we must believe that he had three names, just as Simon Peter and the sons of Zebedee, boanerges, were named from the firmness and greatness of their faith. …
6:2: But the Pharisees, seeing it, said to him: Behold, your disciples are doing what it is not lawful for them to do on the Sabbaths. Note that the first apostles of the Savior destroy the letter of the Sabbath, against the Ebionites, who, though they receive the other apostles, reject Paul as a transgressor of the law.
6:20: Blessed are the poor in spirit. This is what we read elsewhere: And he will save the humble in spirit. But lest anyone should think that poverty, which is sometimes borne of necessity, is being proclaimed by the Lord, he added in spirit, so that you would understand humility, not want. Blessed are the poor in spirit, who for the sake of the Holy Spirit are poor by their own will. …
6:22: Blessed are you when they curse you and persecute you and say every evil against you, lying. That curse is to be despised, and creates blessedness, which is uttered by the mouth of one who curses falsely. Hence he also specifically defined what the blessed curse is, saying: every curse against you, lying, for my sake. So where Christ is the cause, there a curse is to be desired.
6:41: But why do you see the mote in your brother's eye and do not see the beam in your own eye, and the rest. He speaks of those who, though they are themselves held liable for a mortal crime, do not pardon lesser sins in their brothers, straining out the gnat and swallowing the camel. Rightly, then, these too, as we said above, are called hypocrites for their pretense of justice, who through the beam in their own eye look at the mote in their brother's eye.
6:43: Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad. For the tree is known by its fruits. He binds them with a syllogism which the Greeks call ἄφυκτον, and which we can call inescapable, which, when men are questioned, shuts them in on this side and on that and presses them with either horn. If, he says, the devil is evil, he cannot do good works; but if the things you see done are good, it follows that it is not the devil who does them. …
6:46: Not everyone who says to me: Lord, Lord, will enter into the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. As above he had said that those who had the garment of a good life were not to be received because of the wickedness of their doctrines, so now, conversely, he asserts that credence is not to be given even to those who, though strong in the integrity of the faith, live shamefully and destroy the integrity of their teaching by evil works. …
6:6: And when he had passed on from there, he came into their synagogue. And behold, a man having a withered hand. This man, who is healed in the synagogue, is the thirteenth. And it is to be noted that the hand was withered not on the road and out of doors, but in the assembly of the Jews.
6:7: And they questioned him, saying: Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbaths? so that they might accuse him. Since he had excused by an acceptable example the destruction of the Sabbath which the Pharisees charged against the disciples, they wish to slander him himself, and they ask whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbaths, so that, if he did not heal, they might accuse him of cruelty or of weakness, and if he healed, of transgression.
7:19: Are you he who is to come, or do we look for another? He does not say: Are you he who has come, but Are you he who is to come; and the sense is: Send me word, since I am about to go down to the lower world, whether I ought to announce you to those below as well, I who have announced you to those above, or whether it is not fitting for the Son of God to taste death, and you will send another for these mysteries.
7:20: Why does John send his disciples to the Lord to ask him: Are you the one who is coming, or should we expect another? (Matthew 11:3 and Luke 7:20) When he had previously said about the same person: Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world. (John 1:29) We have spoken more fully on this question in the Commentaries of Matthew. Therefore, it is clear that you do not have these books yourself, since you ask such questions. …
7:23: And blessed is he who has not been scandalized in me, he strikes at the go-betweens, as will be shown in what follows.
7:31: But to what shall I liken this generation? It is like children sitting in the forum, who call out to their companions and say: We sang to you, and you did not dance; we lamented to you, and you did not mourn. For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say: He has a demon. The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say: Look, a gluttonous man and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners. And wisdom has been justified by her children. …
7:33: Nor is it surprising if you have despised the twofold way of salvation, when you have spurned fasting and fullness alike. If fasting pleases you, why did John displease you? If fullness, why the Son of Man? Of these you called the one a man with a demon, the other a glutton and a drunkard. …
7:8: Behold, I, though I am a man, say to this one: Go, and he goes, and the rest. He wishes to show that the Lord too could accomplish what he wished not only through the coming of his body but through the ministries of angels.
8:10: Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see and hearing they do not hear. He says these things of those who stand on the shore and are separated from Jesus, and, with the sound of the waves roaring, do not hear clearly what is said, and in them is fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah: By hearing you shall hear and shall not understand, and seeing you shall see and shall not see. These things were prophesied of the crowds that stand on the shore and do not deserve to hear the word of God. …
8:12: The evil one comes and snatches what has been sown in his heart. The evil one snatches the good seed. And at the same time understand that it was sown in the heart, and that the different kinds of ground are the souls of believers.
8:13: But when tribulation and persecution have come because of the word, he is at once scandalized. Pay attention to what is said: he is at once scandalized. There is therefore some difference between the one who is compelled by many tribulations and punishments to deny Christ and the one who at the first persecution is immediately scandalized and falls.
8:14: But he who sows among thorns, this is he who hears the word, and the care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches chokes the word, and it is made fruitless. It seems to me that what is said to Adam according to the letter, Among thorns and thistles you shall eat your bread, also signifies mystically that whoever gives himself to the pleasures of the world and the cares of this world eats the heavenly bread and the true food among thorns. And he aptly added: the deceitfulness of riches chokes the word. …
8:15: But he who was sown in good ground, this is he who hears the word and understands and bears fruit. Just as in the bad ground there were three different kinds, the wayside and the rocky and the thorny places, so in the good ground there is a threefold diversity: of the hundredfold, the sixtyfold and the thirtyfold fruit. And in the one as in the other it is not the substance that is changed but the will, and it is the hearts of unbelievers as well as of believers that receive the seed. …
8:18: He who has, it will be given to him, and he will abound; but he who does not have, even what he has will be taken from him. It is not by an equality of judgment that something is added to those who have, and that from those who do not have even what they seem to have is taken away; rather, to the apostles, who have faith in Christ, something is granted, even if they have somewhat fewer virtues, while from the Jews, who did not believe in the Son of God, it is taken away, even if they possess something through the …
8:19: While he was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and his brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak to him. And someone said to him: Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside seeking you. The Lord was occupied in the work of the word, in the teaching of the peoples, in the duty of preaching; his mother and brothers come and stand outside and desire to speak to him. Then someone announces to the Savior that his mother and brothers are standing outside seeking him. …
8:28: What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us? This confession is not one of will, on which the reward of confessing follows, but an extortion of necessity, which compels the unwilling; just as runaway slaves, if after a long time they see their master, beg for nothing else but to be spared the lash, so too the demons, seeing the Lord suddenly dwelling on earth, believed that he had come to judge them. The presence of the Savior is the torment of the demons. …
8:4: And he spoke many things to them in parables, saying. The crowd is not of one mind but of wills differing in each person. Hence he speaks to it in many parables, so that according to their various wills they might receive different teachings. And it should be noted that he did not speak all things to them in parables, but many. For if he had said everything in parables, the people would have gone away without profit. …
8:52: And when Jesus had come into the ruler's house and had seen the flute players and the crowd in an uproar. To this day the girl lies dead in the ruler's house, and those who seem to be teachers are flute players singing a mournful song. The crowd of the Jews, too, is not a crowd of believers but a crowd of people in an uproar.
8:8: He who has ears to hear, let him hear. We are roused to the understanding of what is said whenever we are admonished by these words.
8:9: And the disciples came and said to him. It must be asked how the disciples come to him when Jesus is sitting in the ship, unless perhaps we are given to understand that some time before they had gone up into the ship with him and, standing there, had inquired about the interpretation of the parable.
9:1: And having called together his twelve disciples, he gave them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every sickness and every infirmity. The kind and merciful Lord and Master does not begrudge his servants and disciples his own mighty works, and just as he himself had healed every sickness and every infirmity, so he grants to his apostles too the power to heal every sickness and every infirmity. But there is a great difference between having and granting, between giving and receiving. …
9:12: But when evening had come, his disciples came to him, saying, and the rest. All things are full of mysteries. He withdraws from Judea, he comes into a desert place, the crowds follow him, having left their cities, Jesus comes out to them, he has pity on the crowd, he heals their sick; and he does this not in the morning, not as the day grows, not at midday, but in the evening, when the sun of justice had set.
9:13: They answered him: We have nothing here but five loaves and two fishes. In another evangelist we read: There is a certain boy here who has five loaves, and he seems to me to signify Moses; the two fishes we understand either as both Testaments, or because an even number refers to the law. So the apostles, before the passion of the Savior and the flashing forth of the lightning-bright Gospel, had nothing but five loaves and two little fishes, which moved about in salt waters and in bitter waves.
9:17: And they took up of the remnants twelve baskets full of fragments. Each of the apostles fills his basket from the Savior's remnants, either so that he may have from it something with which afterwards to offer food to the Gentiles, or so that he may teach from the remnants that those were real loaves which were afterwards multiplied. And at the same time ask how, in the desert and in so vast a solitude, no loaves are found but five only, and two little fishes, and yet twelve baskets are found so easily.
9:19: And they said: Some John the Baptist, others Elijah, but others Jeremiah or one of the prophets. I wonder at certain interpreters who inquire into the causes of each one's errors and weave a very long discussion of why some thought our Lord Jesus Christ to be John, others Elijah, but others Jeremiah or one of the prophets, when they could have erred thus about Elijah and Jeremiah in the same way that Herod erred about John, saying: John, whom I beheaded, has himself risen from the dead, and mighty works are at …
9:2: And going, preach, saying that the kingdom of heaven has drawn near; heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons; freely you have received, freely give. So that rustic men, without the charm of eloquence, unlearned and unlettered, should not go unbelieved when they promised the kingdoms of heaven, he gives them power: heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons, so that the greatness of the signs might prove the greatness of the promises.
9:20: But whom do you say that I am? Simon Peter answered: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. Prudent reader, observe that from what follows and from the texture of the discourse the apostles are by no means called men but gods. For when he had said: Whom do men say that the Son of Man is, he added: But whom do you say that I am? Since they, being men, think human things, you who are gods, whom do you consider me to be? …
9:21: Then he commanded his disciples that they should tell no one that he himself was Jesus Christ. Above, when sending the disciples to preach, he had ordered them to announce his coming; here he commands them not to say that he is Jesus Christ. It seems to me that it is one thing to preach Christ, another to preach Jesus Christ. Christ is a common name of dignity; Jesus is the proper name of the Savior. …
9:22: From then on Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and scribes and chief priests, and be killed, and on the third day rise again. Now the sense is: Preach me then, when I have suffered these things, because it does no good to preach Christ publicly and to spread abroad among the peoples the majesty of him whom a little later they are to see scourged and crucified, suffering many things from the elders and scribes and chief priests. …
9:23: There is also a certain praiseworthy denial, of which the Apostle himself says: "That, denying impiety and worldly desires, we may live purely and justly and piously in this present age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of our Savior God" (Titus 2:12). Whoever denies with this denial, and is willing to follow the Savior when he says, "Whoever will come to me, let him deny himself" (Luke 9:23), having put off the old man with his works and put on the new, will follow his God. …
9:26: For the Son of Man is to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will render to each according to his work. Peter, scandalized at the announcement of the Lord's death, had been rebuked by the Lord's judgment; the disciples were challenged to deny themselves and take up their cross and follow their master in the spirit of men going to their death. Great was the terror of the hearers, and such as could, with the chief of the apostles terrified, cast fear into the others too. …
9:27: Amen I say to you: There are some of those standing here who shall not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. He had wished to heal the terror of the apostles with the hope of what was promised, saying: The Son of Man is to come in the glory of his Father with his angels; adding besides the authority of the judge: And he will render to each according to his works. …
9:28: And after six days Jesus took Peter and James and John his brother. Why Peter and James and John are separated from the rest in certain places of the Gospels, or what privilege they have beyond the other apostles, we have often said. Now it is asked how he took them after six days and led them up a high mountain apart, when Luke the evangelist puts the number eight. But the answer is easy: here the middle days are given; there the first and the last are added. …
9:29:
And he was transfigured before them. Such as he is to be at the time of judging, such he appeared to the apostles. But as to his saying: he was transfigured before them, let no one think that he lost his former form and face, or gave up the reality of his body and took on a body either spiritual or airy; but how he was transformed the evangelist shows, saying:

And his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white as snow. …
9:30: And behold, there appeared to them Moses and Elijah, talking with him. When the scribes and Pharisees were testing him and demanding signs from heaven, he would not give them, but refuted the perverse demand with a prudent answer. Here, however, to increase the faith of the apostles, he gives a sign from heaven, Elijah coming down from the place to which he had ascended, and Moses rising from the underworld; as Ahaz too is instructed through Isaiah to ask for himself a sign from on high or from hell. …
9:34: And the disciples, hearing it, fell on their face and were exceedingly afraid. They are struck with dread for a threefold cause: either because they had recognized that they had erred, or because the bright cloud had covered them, or because they had heard the voice of God the Father speaking; human frailty does not endure to bear the sight of a greater glory, and, trembling in its whole soul and body, it falls to the earth. …
9:36: And as they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying: Tell the vision to no one until the Son of Man rises from the dead. A foretaste of the kingdom to come and the glory of the one triumphing had been shown on the mountain. He does not wish, therefore, that this be preached among the peoples, lest it both be incredible because of the greatness of the thing and, after such great glory, the cross that followed should cause a stumbling block among untaught minds.
9:38: Lord, have mercy on my son, for he is a lunatic and suffers badly; for he often falls into the fire, and frequently into the water; and I brought him to your disciples, and they could not cure him. For what reason a demon, watching the course of the moon, seizes men and strives through the creatures to defame the Creator, we have said above. …
9:4: Into whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and stay there until you leave. Concerning the ordination of a bishop and a deacon Paul says: Moreover they must also have a good testimony from those who are outside. The apostles, entering a new city, could not know who was of what sort. Therefore the host is to be chosen by the report of the people and the judgment of the neighbors, lest the dignity of the preaching be disfigured by the ill repute of the one who receives them. …
9:40: But as to his saying: I brought him to your disciples, and they could not cure him, he covertly accuses the apostles, although the impossibility of curing is sometimes to be referred not to the weakness of those who cure but to the faith of those who are to be cured, as the Lord says: Be it done to you according to your faith.
9:41: Jesus answered and said: O unbelieving and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I bear with you? Not that he was overcome by weariness, and that he who is meek and gentle, who like a lamb before its shearer did not open his mouth, broke out into words of fury; but that, in the likeness of a physician who sees a sick man conducting himself against his orders, he might say: How long shall I come to your house, how long shall I waste the diligence of my art, when I order one thing and you …
9:42: And Jesus rebuked him, and the demon went out of him. Not he who was suffering but the demon ought to have been rebuked. Or else he rebuked the boy, and the demon went out of him, because he had been oppressed by the demon on account of his own sins.
9:44: And while they were staying in Galilee, Jesus said to them: The Son of Man is to be betrayed into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again. And they were exceedingly saddened. He always mingles sadness with prosperous things, so that when these come suddenly they may not terrify the apostles, but may be borne by minds that have prepared for them beforehand. …
9:46: At that hour the disciples came to Jesus, saying: Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven? What I have often advised must be observed now too: the causes of each of the Lord's sayings and deeds are to be sought. After the stater was found, after the tribute was paid, what does this sudden question of the apostles mean? At that hour the disciples came to Jesus, saying: Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven? …
9:47: And Jesus, calling a little child, set him in their midst. Either simply any little child, so that he might seek out that age and show the likeness of innocence; or else he set himself in their midst as the little child, he who had come not to be served but to serve, so that he might give them an example of humility. Others interpret the little child as the Holy Spirit, whom he placed in the hearts of the disciples so that they might exchange pride for humility.
9:48: Whoever therefore humbles himself like this little child, he is greater in the kingdom of heaven. Just as this little child, whose example I give you, does not persist in anger, does not remember when he has been hurt, is not delighted at the sight of a beautiful woman, does not think one thing and say another, so you too, unless you have such innocence and purity of mind, will not be able to enter the kingdom of heaven. …
9:5: And whoever does not receive you nor hear your words, going outside, out of the house or the city, shake off the dust from your feet. The dust is shaken from the feet as a testimony of their labor, that they entered the city and the apostolic preaching reached even to them; or else the dust is shaken off so that they may accept nothing, not even what is necessary for food, from those who have spurned the Gospel.
9:53: What is the meaning of what is written in the Gospel according to Luke: "And they did not receive him: because his face was going to Jerusalem" (Luke 9:53). Hastening, the Lord went to Jerusalem to fulfill the days of his assumption and to celebrate the Passover, about which he had said: "With desire I have desired to eat this Pasch with you, before I suffer" (Ibid. 22:15), and drink the cup, of which he said: "The cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?" (John 18:11). …
9:57: And a scribe came up and said to him: Master, I will follow you wherever you go. And Jesus says to him: Foxes have holes and the birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. This scribe of the law, who knew only the letter that kills, if he had said: Lord, I will follow you wherever you go, would not have been rejected by the Lord; but because he reckoned him one master among many, and was a man of letters (which is more expressively said in Greek γραμματεύς, and not a spiritual hearer), …
9:59: And another of his disciples said to him: Lord, let me first go and bury my father. What likeness is there between the scribe and the disciple? The one calls him master, the other confesses him Lord; the one, on the occasion of piety, desires to go to bury his father, the other promises that he will follow wherever he goes, seeking not the master but gain from the master.
